speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Quite suddenly, for the first time in history, Singapore was left to take care of its own defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We had barely been independent for six years and were still finding our feet as a nation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The withdrawal of the British forces also had serious economic implications.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Asia, like the rest of the world, was divided by the Cold War conflicts and tensions with wars raging in Vietnam and Korea.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to the neighbourhood, Konfrontasi was still fresh in our memories, as were the communist and communalist riots on the domestic front.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The challenge for a small country is that should it be subject to aggression by a larger country, it will still need to be able to hold its own.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) is now one of the most respected armed forces in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our military leaders perform well in international assignments and our armed forces have made a good name for themselves assisting countries in disaster relief and humanitarian efforts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the purpose of the SAF remains primarily to address security threats and I will highlight a few that remain a concern.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The terrorist attacks in Brussels and Paris are grim reminders of what terrorists are capable of.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The South China Sea tensions continue to escalate despite the fact that the legal dispute resolution process is moving forward – indeed, maybe, it is escalating in response to this process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The latest actions see China reclaiming land, building up defence installations and lighthouses in the region, with the US and Australia continuing to assert their freedom of navigation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Philippines and Vietnam, meanwhile, maintain their claims through the legal process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even more worrying is the Korean Peninsula, where North Korea continues its nuclear testing and, perhaps, for one of the first times I can remember in history, making specific threats to launch a nuclear strike.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may change the face of warfare if that were to materialise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, the Straits of Malacca continues to have stories of piracy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Their plan was foiled when they were spotted by security forces, but they managed to slip away in a lifeboat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a small, interconnected country, Singapore is likely to be affected by these threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will be interested to know what the Ministry of Defence's (MINDEF's) views are, both in relation to the threats I have described as well as what they believe to be the most salient national security challenges Singapore faces today?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Threats today come from states, organisations and individuals that seek to undermine our security.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, Minister Ng Eng Hen spoke extensively on hybrid warfare and he described hybrid warfare as the exact antagonist of Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is precisely because of the tools of coercion and aggression that these are wide-ranging, and their being wide-ranging means it may be difficult for nations, such as Singapore, to even identify the source of attacks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While traditional battlefields of the past were largely confined to air, land and sea domains, modern conflicts have moved into other domains that extend beyond territorial and geographical boundaries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, what are some of these trends that MINDEF has observed and are we facing such threats in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Has Singapore been tested by such threats in recent months?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is clear that the military solution is not sufficient to address the threat of hybrid warfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, how is the Government responding to the threat of warfare on the various fronts and how do we bring in the stakeholders in Total Defence on board?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We were quite good in having thought through Total Defence for many years, but given how things have evolved since its inception many years ago, how do we take it to the next level?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have all followed the news reports of recent attacks in Lahore, Brussels, Istanbul.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But those attacks represent just a fraction of the total number that has been carried out in recent months.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Regarding ISIS in particular, some analysts have observed that there has been a shift in the group's strategy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A recent Financial Times' article noted that beyond creating a caliphate in Iraq and Syria, ISIS is looking to strengthen its caliphate further afield and export terror to its perceived enemies beyond the Middle East.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many continue to travel to Iraq to Syria to fight for the ISIS cause in the Middle East.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most alarmingly, however, analysts have also pointed out that ISIS' tactics are also shifting.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ISIS has been encouraging its supporters, some of whom had never travelled to the Middle East, to conduct attacks in their home cities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without specific operational direction, lone wolves and small wolf packs have been inspired into action by ISIS' general call.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some have obtained weapons or explosives capable of causing mass casualties.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is clearly an alarming trend for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the wake of the recent series of attacks in various cities, militaries have stepped up, alongside law enforcement agencies, to respond to the heightened risk.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Military patrols have also been deployed in countries, such as France, Belgium and Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, my question is: what are MINDEF's and the SAF's roles in preventing and responding to terrorist attacks?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Traditionally, SAF has focused its preparations on external threats while the Home Team has focused on homeland security matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I believe the military's role in homeland defence should be carefully calibrated, as deploying the military would send a clear message to the public that the threat is a serious one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: If used for minor threats, the public may get the wrong message and get unduly worried or panic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the other hand, if used in a situation where panic has already ensued following the attack, it may help calm the situation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Are there any plans for SAF to step up its responses to homeland security to deal with threats, such as terrorism?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Sri Lanka has since managed to trace around $20 million and returned these sums.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But the money channeled to the Philippines, amounting to some $80 million, still remains untraced.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Clearly, the figures that were transferred out were staggering and a demonstration of the power of hackers being able to get through government institutions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, it is very clear that states can become victims of cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: An equally worrying trend is that the power of hacking is also being harnessed by state actors, too, including countries that are supposed to be friendly with each other.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: News, for example, of the German Chancellor Angela Merkel's phone being hacked by the US National Security Agency created diplomatic tensions between countries that were otherwise very good friends.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But this may be a microcosm of state-sponsored hacking that is probably happening elsewhere as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given that cyber threats are on the rise and state actors can be both victims as well as the responsible parties, does MINDEF have plans to develop capabilities to counter this threat?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: As we know, e-commerce and communications have increased relevance in Singapore and we are becoming more and more reliant on it in the way we work, play and even in many aspects of the activities that we undertake.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And particularly in Singapore, with our vision of becoming a smarter nation, cybersecurity is increasingly of concern.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The spectrum of cybercrime can range from highly sophisticated syndicates or to a lone wolf hacker or even a youngster who cannot just resist the chance to crack a password or hack a computer system.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This man had hacked into the user accounts simply by guessing, I guess, through an algorithm, the login passwords of these users.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is fortunate in this case that the incident did not result in even more damage.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Had the cyber perpetrator been a terrorist network, more harm could be inflicted.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: What measures are in place to prevent them?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And if an attack does occur, especially affecting essential services like energy, water and banking, how would we be able to respond to them?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: What are our disaster recovery plans and business continuity measures?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Such capabilities are important today, given the network-centric nature of contemporary society and, indeed, military operations today.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I have three sets of questions for MINDEF on these matters.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Cyberattacks need not simply be about conventional military operations.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: They can involve everything from gathering and corrupting sensitive information to disabling vulnerable civilian infrastructure, such as public utilities, communications, financial systems, emergency and medical response, business infrastructure and even transportation management systems.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: These actions can disrupt society and make it susceptible to pressure.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How does MINDEF's cyber defence address these issues?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How does MINDEF intend to ensure that Singapore is well-protected?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Further, like other military systems, cyber defence capabilities may raise suspicions and tensions with neighbours that can, ultimately, make the nation less secure.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How does MINDEF plan to mitigate this risk as it develops its cyber defence capabilities?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, cyber defence tools are powerful and hard to detect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How does MINDEF ensure that there is sufficient oversight of its systems to prevent inappropriate use by other individuals or Government agencies?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Can MINDEF assure the public on this matter, such as by issuing an annual report or audit on cyber risks, breaches and mitigation efforts?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: While the Ministry of Foreign Affairs manages official diplomatic ties between countries, our armed forces have also played an important role in building relations with counterparts in other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These ties have helped us get access to training spaces abroad, opportunities to train together with foreign armed forces and, perhaps most importantly, to build good relations with our counterparts and foreign militaries so that we will have friends should the need ever arise.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng, you have three cuts.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is, therefore, for very good reasons that Singapore shares long-standing defence ties with Malaysia, Indonesia as well as Brunei.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is known that senior MINDEF and SAF officials meet with their counterparts regularly.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: SAF also engages in regular bilateral exercises, high-level visits and professional exchanges.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With changes in leadership, developments in geopolitical situation, set in the context of an evolving regional and international security scene, how have our ties kept up with the times and different priorities?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I would also like to ask MINDEF for an update on the state of our bilateral defence relationships with our immediate neighbours.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What are some recent exchanges that have taken place and how have these enhanced the interests of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: On defence and security, CSP will build on strong existing ties between Singapore and Australia's defence establishments.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Singapore and Australia are part of the Five-Power Defence Arrangements and both countries' armed forces have deployed alongside each other in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Australia currently hosts military training by the Singapore Army and RSAF.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What has been achieved and what are some new areas of practical cooperation being explored through such multilateral fora?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With the realisation of ASEAN Community 2015, how will ASEAN bring regional defence cooperation to new heights?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In that respect, can MINDEF share how ASEAN members have worked together in recent regional disasters like the Sabah earthquake?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The current regional security landscape is also characterised by non-traditional security challenges, such as maritime security and the rise of violence and brutality committed by extremist organisations and radical groups.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How are the multilateral fora helping Singapore to be better prepared for these new challenges?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Likewise, Singapore needs to ensure that we are still as capable and as ready to respond to such threats.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Threats to our sovereignty as a proud nation should not be tolerated and our security should never be compromised.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that in mind, I would like to ask the Minister if SAF's approach to defence spending has changed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there plans to increase defence spending at a faster pace and what are the new areas that we are focusing on in our defence spending?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, what is sometimes not so well understood is the impact such white papers can have on improving and building confidence and trust among countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In an S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) commentary this year, a local researcher noted that Australia's 2016 white paper sent a strong positive signal to Southeast Asia and potentially contributes to the region's stability and peace.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was quite telling that the former Minister for Defence, Mr Lee Boon Yang, in 1995, quoted verbatim a section of the Australian defence white paper in this House, as a measure of the good relations between the two countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is my view that the wider publication of such initiatives through a white paper would serve MINDEF's interests, both nationally and internationally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MINDEF, as the largest consumer of the national Budget, will always be queried about the nature and scale of its defence expenditure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These demands will grow and are not likely to abate in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, the section on the Ministry of Law, a far smaller Ministry budget-wise, has more than 40 pages long.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is no requirement for MINDEF to release any secret information in the prospective White Paper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the current state of affairs is more than opaque, especially in an economic environment post-SG50, which ought to be marked by greater fiscal prudence in light of multiple national priorities, all worthy of equal consideration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A White Paper will put into perspective MINDEF's mission and requirements the one hand, and its budgetary needs on the other, in the context of the needs of a small state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I am not suggesting a need to do this, the point is that a White Paper offers great flexibility for MINDEF to determine how best to get its message out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Japanese experience with white papers is quite telling, as it moves from a limited paper in 2015 to a much more comprehensive one last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A MINDEF White Paper can be even used to showcase the seriousness MINDEF takes in its safety regime, something I will talk about in my next cut.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Not a month passes without some blasts, wars, disputes somewhere, which affect many innocent citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These are all major concerns for nations, including Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: National militaries around the world are all on high alert.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How does MINDEF ensure our armed forces stay relevant and attuned to the changing security environment and climate, with the background of all these challenges?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How prepared are we to respond to such threats as a small nation with a small army?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What are the other roles our personnel can play to help step up deterrence levels?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Jessica Tan, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The SAF does pride itself in possessing cutting-edge capabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is the range of the local defence technology capabilities that we have?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How are these capabilities contributing to the technology edge and indigenous technology science capabilities of SAF?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And with the competing demands on engineering talent at the national level, what efforts is MINDEF making to ensure that it continues to have the required engineering talent and capabilities to build on our indigenous defence, science and technology capabilities?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have seen heightened security concerns in the region and globally.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With greater uncertainty and a wider spectrum of threats, including conventional as well as asymmetric threats, such as terrorism and cyber warfare, how then does the SAF ensure that our defence forces are operationally ready?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is the operational value of regular training that SAF conducts overseas?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In what ways do these trainings give us the assurance that they, indeed, prepare our forces?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is the objective of these overseas exercises in countries like the US, Australia, Germany, France and New Zealand?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These countries differ in many aspects from our local and regional conditions, such as climate, landscape and vegetation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Such overseas training exercises do impact citizen soldiers as well as cost of operations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is the SAF doing to ensure that our society will continue to support this commitment to defence?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To participate in such overseas exercises, our soldiers will need to be away from their families and work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we need to achieve training effectiveness, how does the SAF balance the impact on work, family and opportunities for our citizen soldiers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the disruption, pace of change and the need for continual learning and skills upgrading, how would the SAF respond to support our citizen soldiers as they face these changes in competing demands with the need of overseas training and operational requirements?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: SAF was established in 1965, as Members know, a necessity created by Singapore's Independence, with the primary focus on providing for Singapore's external defence.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Today, our 3rd Generation SAF is widely known to be well-equipped to defend Singapore against external threats.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: The SAF is well-respected as a strong and professional armed forces.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: It underwrites Singapore's sovereignty upon which all Singaporeans can live in peace and secure in the knowledge that Singapore is well-protected.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: However, the threats facing Singapore have broadened beyond conventional war to areas like counter-terrorism, piracy and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR).

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: So, I would like the Minister to help us to understand how the SAF is preparing to confront the new challenges that I have described.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: In 2015, Singapore assisted in various missions, such as fighting forest fires in Chiang Mai, Thailand and Sumatra, and also search-and-rescue operations in Nepal as a result of the earthquake.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Many Singaporeans are proud of our SAF and the Home Team personnel who participated in these HADR efforts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Situations today are increasingly volatile and news of newfound threats always seems to be getting a little closer to home.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Understandably, this will cause some worry amongst our citizens.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Today's threats do not present themselves until the last minute and, by the time they do, we have seen how it is often just a little too late in other countries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: While the SAF may be prepared to defend Singapore against today's threats, these threats – like everything else – will continue to evolve as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Our approach to defence has not been about keeping up, but always ensuring that we are not one but several steps ahead.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: This provides us with the two-pronged benefit of deterring those who may mean to harm us, and also ensuring that we are able to react swiftly and decisively to any threat.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Can MINDEF provide an update on the SAF's transformation plans?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: As our threats evolve, so should our defence capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: The consequences of failure on this part are extremely grave and we cannot afford to be complacent on this issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How do we ensure we can maximise their potential?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We have also strategically, over the years, developed our capabilities in terms of a 4G-SAF and specialisation skillsets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Technological capabilities and enhancements have also been very active as well.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think they have made their points eloquently, many valid points and accurate observations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Collectively, they bring home this truth that as much as all of us want peace, work for greater cooperation and understanding among countries, neither the world nor the region we live in is Utopia; that each generation of Singaporeans will face threats, and each generation will have to renew their commitment to protect what they value or lose it; that we can only depend on ourselves to defend Singapore; that we will need to work with other like-minded partners to deal with potential troubles along the way.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singapore and Singaporeans will have to gear up for "troubled peace" in this new era after SG50.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Each generation of Singaporeans will have to confront their own security threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The founding generation, as Mr Vikram Nair pointed out, did not have it easy.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, the 1960s and 1970s, as he said, were tumultuous times in Asia and, especially, for Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Whether it was Konfrontasi or the ideological battles against communism and communalism, these contests often led to violence or subversion.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And because Southeast Asian states were newly-minted nations in the 1960s and 1970s, only recently freed from their colonial past, individual nations were more preoccupied with their national agendas, rather than cooperating as a region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Geopolitics today has improved, and we talked about ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ASEAN is an accepted regional community in international dynamics.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ASEAN has good growth and strong relations with other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But despite this progress, as Members have said, challenges exist.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef noted that we live in an interconnected world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And, indeed, what happens in some other part of the world, many Members have said that it occurs very far away but comes closer to home, as Mr Zainal Sapari said, whether it is terrorism or technological warfare.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And as Mr Vikram Nair noted, there have been numerous developments recently in the South China Sea, more terrorist attacks, and a sophisticated cyberattack involving the US Federal Reserve.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have asked key questions − Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Low Thia Khiang, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Ms Low Yen Ling, Mr Cedric Foo and Mr Zainal Sapari.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In summary, they asked: what are the main security threats to Singapore and how significant are they when compared to previous years?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: How is the SAF responding to these threats?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: How can we keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These are all important questions that can change our lives here irrevocably.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I agree completely with Mr Zainal Sapari when he said that the consequences of failure will be great.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, I intend to answer these questions in the course of this reply for the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As of now, there is no specific intelligence of any imminent plot against Singapore, but the general assessment by our intelligence agencies indicates that almost all cities are likely targets, including Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members here already know of attacks in other cities in the past 18 months – Paris, Sydney, San Bernardino, Istanbul, Bangkok, Jakarta, Brussels and, most recently, Lahore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: A few months later, you may have to add more cities to that list.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, our assessment is that the threat levels from ISIS are higher than that from AQ and JI.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ISIS controls territories and oil fields in Iraq and Syria from which they can draw resources to fund tens of thousands of fighters and further its goals.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ISIS even uses drones for its operations, like a military.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They can orchestrate and coordinate attacks far away, as they did in Paris, Brussels or even near us, Jakarta.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is a Malay Archipelago Combat Unit, and ISIS had given them S$100,000 to finance terrorist attacks and bombings in Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ISIS operatives and sympathisers have already formed networks in our region, as some Members have observed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And more have been radicalised without even travelling to the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Most recently, Members would have read that four Singaporeans were prevented from joining the armed conflicts in the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Members have pointed out, returning fighters will bring back their extremist ideology, share their experience in weapons, explosives and actual fighting.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In addition, we know that they have linked up with existing cells, like the JI offshoot, Jamaah Ansharut Tauhid, and Abu Sayyaf.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In our region, ISIS has declared its mission to establish a wilayat, a "caliphate", and Katibah Nusantara is leading the charge.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This central ideology of a Southeast Asian "caliphate" binds Islamic militants who have already set up training camps in Sulawesi, Aceh and in the Southern Philippines.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even the Uighurs are known to have joined a training camp in Sulawesi, led by the Indonesian militant, Santoso.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I am not sure what the tenuous connections had been previously between militants in Indonesia and the Uighurs, but here, you have it − that ideology binds them together.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In this narrative, Singapore is an attractive target.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Every shopping mall, every crowded place is an opportunity for violent extremists to target innocent civilians and cause as much suffering and mayhem as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ISIS operatives and sympathisers, especially what we call "clean skins" – those with no prior criminal record – can travel and smuggle components of arms and explosives.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has stepped up security checks, but the terrorists only need to succeed once.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Under these circumstances, can Singapore – or, for that matter, any city – guarantee its residents that no extremist attack will occur?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think the answer is an obvious one.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Only a foolish and complacent government will provide that false sense of security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Instead, we must step up our defences, bring our citizens into confidence and, more importantly, confront this threat and prepare to deal with the aftermath together.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I will elaborate on how SAF will respond to this.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But even as we ask Singaporeans to prepare ourselves to deal with extremist threats, let me just say that we must be mindful, at the same time, of the trajectory of state-to-state relations surrounding us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Members have pointed out, the disputes in the South China Sea and East China Sea are increasing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They are symptomatic of a more powerful dynamic of strategic rivalry and rising nationalism.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This state of flux, different from post-World War II, different from the Cold War, is creating tension.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This dynamic will stress existing military cooperation and alliances; it will stress international agreements or laws, even the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On a regular basis, Japanese fighter jets scramble in response to the People's Liberation Army (PLA) military aircraft that enter Japan's Air Defence Identification Zone (ADIZ).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The PLA planes are flying into disputed airspace around the Diao Yu/Senkaku Islands.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, the Japanese would have to respond, and they scramble.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The largest overlap in the South China Sea claims is between Vietnam's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and China's "nine dash line".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members would recall that just two years ago, Vietnamese and Chinese vessels clashed over an oil rig in the South China Sea.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And you would remember that, in Vietnam, they held protests and burned down foreign-owned factories, meaning to target Chinese-owned factories.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They hear them speak in Mandarin, and so, they got burnt.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just recently, the Vietnamese coast guard seized a Chinese oil tanker allegedly operating in Vietnam's waters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And for the first time ever − if you have not noticed this − a Japanese submarine arrived in Cam Ranh International Port.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It called in Vietnam last month for the first time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: An example closer to home: the Indonesian Government has also taken a hard stance against illegal fishing in its EEZ.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just last month, there was a standoff between the Chinese coast guard and an Indonesian patrol vessel.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indonesia has since announced plans to deploy fighter jets to the Natuna Islands.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And supposedly, as a show of strength, military ships of the Indonesian National Defence Forces (TNI) are used to blow up these merchant vessels.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Military munitions cost more but, as a show of strength, they will use TNI to blow up the vessels.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As we observed, these incidents are occurring at an increasing regularity.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have to remember that they occur against the backdrop of Asia's highest military spending ever.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But with more capable militaries, miscalculations or missteps can precipitate serious tensions and even physical conflicts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As we look around and look at our security challenges, this troubled peace around us reaffirms our policy on steady and prudent defence spending.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked about this, as well as Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I want to thank Members from all parties here – Non-Constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs) included – for their steadfast support for the defence budgets over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Together, Members in this House were wise not to have taken short periods of peace for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As some Members have pointed out, Singapore, too, could have gone down the path of European countries to reap our own "peace dividend" because the threat of communism had waned and we see ASEAN progressing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But if we had been so lulled into that complacent mood and under-invested in defence capabilities, then, just like countries, such as Finland or the Baltic states, I think we would have regretted it now and rushed to catch up.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But we avoided spikes or dips in our defence spending and maintained a strong SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The next decade would not be easy for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In fact, I believe that the next few decades will pose to Singapore its greatest challenge since our Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have never had a situation where our factors of production are on the decline and our needs are going up.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But even as our population ages and social spending increases, we must maintain steady defence spending because that is the most effective way to stretch every defence dollar.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It allows us to avoid disruptive changes from fluctuating expenditures.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is very difficult, as Mr Sapari has pointed out, and other countries have discovered, to suddenly wake up and say, "Oh, I need a stronger defence because the threats have gone worse" and then quickly expect to build a strong defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This PAP Government will continue to invest wisely and spend prudently on defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For MINDEF, we buy only what the SAF needs, and after a robust and stringent evaluation process.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We do not go around shopping for expensive or highly sophisticated stuff.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We adopt the most cost-effective solution, looking clearly at what we need.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And our first preference is to upgrade existing platforms, if we can do it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For example, like the F-16s, we are going to upgrade them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We only buy new equipment if Singapore needs them to maintain that defence edge.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members have asked how I see our defence expenditure going forward.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Sometimes, it does not get passed on to the equipment we buy so quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Is this era of troubled peace hyped up?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some have questioned: do we really need that kind of defence?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The US, the world's most wealthy democracy with the largest and most capable military, can perhaps take that line and live with the consequences, if something goes wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But for Singapore, a little red dot in the middle of a region with extremist threats, rising nationalism and strategic rivalry, we should guard against the worst and prepare ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, some scholars and even world leaders have suggested that the face of "war" has already changed and is upon us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: According to them, unlike in the past when wars were fought in specific localities, today's conflicts are increasingly borderless, and occur wave after wave.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, against extremism, first there was AQ, 9/11.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But if ISIS is defeated, I believe another group will rise to take its place.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It may not be in Iraq or Syria but there is a host of failed states that an extremist group can gain a geographical foothold in and take the resources, whether it is Libya or other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In cyberattacks and biological pandemics, ground-zero can be anywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We were worried about bird flu in Indonesia; for the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), it was in some parts of the world; Zika virus in some countries; it can arise anywhere and spread very far quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This troubled peace, according to this new narrative, is the new normal in our globalised world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad talked about hybrid warfare that is ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, it is the antithesis of Total Defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And if you think about it, that generation was prescient and very clever in launching Total Defence – this was more than 30 years ago – because hybrid warfare is an orchestrated campaign to weaken and fracture the solidarity of a target nation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is no laughing matter because it is actually being practised.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: According to this doctrine, the aggressor targets a specific country or countries and undertakes a long-term campaign to undermine the civil, economic, social, psychological and military defences.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even online games, which seemingly are innocent, are used to socialise youngsters to their cause, and the shocking propaganda videos of beheadings and burning people go viral and attract more sympathisers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Cyber attacks are integral parts of hybrid warfare.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Last December, unidentified hackers attacked Ukraine's power grid and disrupted electricity to a large part of the country for hours.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just imagine our power grid is down, traffic lights are out, power stations fail – you can gut out the country quite easily.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Adversaries can, therefore, cripple key operating systems of target countries, steal their state and people's secrets, invade the hearts and minds of their people, all without stepping foot onto their soil.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members here have asked how the SAF should respond in this new normal of troubled peace.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I am glad to say that there was foresight in leaders in MINDEF and the SAF to have identified these broad challenges more than a decade ago.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Since 9/11, the SAF has stood up task forces to deal with peacetime threats.

speaker: The Chairman
text: These task forces are geared up in high readiness posture, fully manned to respond quickly even with little warning.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There is another task force for homeland security and this is called the Island Defence Task Force and it is operational.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In other words, it safeguards our homeland security with active and NS servicemen protecting key installations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You would have seen them if you are in Changi Airport, if you are working in Jurong Island and Sembawang Wharves.

speaker: The Chairman
text: They regularly conduct patrols with the Home Team and, because they are tasked to deal with real threats, they are armed and given clear rules of engagement.

speaker: The Chairman
text: At sea, the Maritime Security Task Force protects our waterways, and the Air Defence Task Force keeps a close watch over our skies.

speaker: The Chairman
text: After the 2008 Mumbai attacks, our response plans were again strengthened to tighten our linkages with home-front and other Government agencies.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have assessed, as we said, the rising threat of terrorism.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In the next few months, the SAF will redouble our efforts to gear up for counter-terrorism.

speaker: The Chairman
text: First, studying what happened in Paris, Jakarta and Brussels, the SAF will enhance its incident response.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some Members have asked: can we use technology?

speaker: The Chairman
text: The SAF is working with our defence engineers and scientists to equip these special forces with better tactical sensors like micro-Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), perhaps small enough to fit in your palm and well-suited for urban terrain.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will continue to develop new technologies and tools that will give the SAF an edge in this fight against terror.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In this, working with the Home Team closely and seamlessly is crucial if we are to bring to bear the full strength of our security capabilities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: SAF is working closely to share intelligence and develop joint operational command systems.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Last year, Exercise High Crest was conducted to validate our whole-of-Government response to simultaneous maritime security threats.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In that exercise, various agencies, the Singapore Police Force (SPF), the Home Team, SAF, the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF), the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) and the Maritime and Port Authority (MPA), worked together to intercept a terrorist speedboat, storm a hijacked merchant vessel and deal with the aftermath.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Second, more SAF units will be trained to take on a wider range of security tasks.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We do not assume, as Ms Low Yen Ling says, that attacks will only be carried out by lone wolves or wolf packs – smaller groups – like those which occurred in Jakarta.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We must be able to deal with orchestrated attacks, like those which occurred in Paris and Brussels, where airports, mass rapid transit (MRT) stations, shopping malls and town centres are targeted simultaneously.

speaker: The Chairman
text: To deal with these scenarios, more SAF units will be trained to conduct deterrence patrols in populous areas.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think that is a question that some Members asked, including Mr Cedric Foo.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I agree with Members that for SAF soldiers to competently undertake this range of missions, we will have to continue to invest in new and realistic training facilities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And that will provide a highly realistic training ground for counter-terrorism as well as conventional urban operations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But as some Members rightly pointed out, beyond our homeland response here, we need to address the threat at its source.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Because only when the source of the threat and recruitment is diminished or eradicated, can the situation here improve.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If we did not address or diminish the capability of AQ, more cells like JI would flourish.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is why Singapore has been involved in multinational counter-terrorism operations since 2007, first, against AQ in Afghanistan, and now against ISIS.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Last year, the SAF deployed our KC-135R tanker to support air-to-air refuelling operations, and we also deployed an Imagery Analysis Team (IAT).

speaker: The Chairman
text: This IAT is tasked to monitor suspected terrorist facilities and activities to help the coalition partners in disrupting supply chains that feed terror networks here.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Even as the SAF gears up for troubled peace and the present threat of terrorism, the SAF will continue to conduct realistic exercises at a high tempo to maintain a strong deterrence.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Members, such as Ms Jessica Tan, have asked about this, whether they are important.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will tell Members that they are very important because that is where we can validate our capabilities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Singapore is not very large to train in.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Training exercises might be finished in 15 minutes if you are going at that speed.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We need the large space because we have so many platforms, so many different units working to bring it together and say, "Would it work?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Can we learn from the mistakes?" So, we need the places, as we do in the US in Exercise Forging Sabre, and Exercise Wallaby in Australia and Exercise Cope Tiger in Thailand, not only to validate our systems, but in joint exercises to benchmark our own capabilities and to show others our capabilities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Because when the SAF is able to perform in exercises, people will take us seriously.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will continue these exercises and we want to make sure that they are mindful of NSmen's commitments.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Even the NSmen who have gone, when I talked to them after their exercises, they feel motivated.

speaker: The Chairman
text: They feel, "Oh, I did something, I can manoeuvre here".

speaker: The Chairman
text: I remember visiting some of them in Bionixes, and they said, "Here I can manoeuvre a lot, whereas in Singapore, you know, it is short circuits".

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some Members have pointed out that piracy has occurred in the Straits of Malacca as well as the South China Sea.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We believe that we should help contain piracy in any part of the world and, so, we are in the Gulf of Aden.

speaker: The Chairman
text: As Members have pointed out, we may be called to help in Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) missions and peace support operations like the Nepal earthquake and the forest fires in Chiang Mai and Palembang, and we will train for that – something which Mr Cedric Foo asked about.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will look at not only training, but set-up structures, which is why we started the Regional HADR Coordination Centre in Changi.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some of you have asked about shrinking manpower pools and how we can address this.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef noted the demographic trends and Ms Jessica Tan asked how technology can continue to be used to maintain the SAF's edge.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I agree with the Members that it is a vital tool, without which we cannot multiply our efforts.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Just as with the recipients of the SAF Scholarship, those who take up this SAF Engineering Scholarship will be able to depart for their university studies earlier, so that, on their return, they can apply their specialised skills and knowledge to the SAF as military engineers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is important because they will form the next generation of leaders in our engineering corps to ensure that we maintain an edge in defence technology.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some Members – Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Zainal Sapari – have asked about hardware.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will continue to refresh and upgrade platforms at a sustainable pace.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is in lieu of a White Paper.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Our SAF is not very big that there will be much more information that I can give in the White Paper than what I am telling Members here.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, if Members see what we have in Changi Naval Base, see what we have in Sungei Gedong, see what we have in the airbases, it is all there.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The fact that we primarily raise the SAF for deterrence, people understand.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are not quite like Australia, which I think needs a White Paper for now and then to, as Mr Pritam Singh say, show others.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For Singapore, for the SAF, we make friends with everyone and our defence is purely for deterrence.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will tell Members that the development is on track.

speaker: The Chairman
text: They will replace the ageing Challenger-class submarines and should be commissioned by 2020.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This year, the Army will also launch a new Protected Combat Support Vehicle to provide better protection and mobility for our supporting troops.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For RSAF, our Super Pumas and some of our Chinooks are ageing and will need to be replaced.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are finalising our evaluations and expect the new RSAF helicopters soon.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will announce it when we finish the evaluations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For the F-16s, as I have said, we are upgrading them with more advanced radars – the Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radars – and air-to-ground weapons.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The SAF will deploy more unmanned platforms, beyond what we already have – the UAVs, so that manpower resources can be freed up for other missions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The Navy envisages that unmanned vessels may eventually complement our ships to patrol our waterways and clear underwater mines.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Likewise, our Army may use Unmanned Ground Vehicles to conduct security patrols.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Low Thia Khiang and Mr Cedric Foo asked about our cyber defences – well put questions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We consider this threat as a very serious one.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It can potentially be more destructive than even physical intrusion, because it can disrupt our key installations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I would say that this is also a national priority.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Nationally, the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) was launched last year under the aegis of the Prime Minister's Office (PMO); overseeing is PMO and Deputy Prime Minister Teo who oversees the National Security Coordination Secretariat (NSCS).

speaker: The Chairman
text: For those in this business, it is not tens; it is not hundreds; it is not thousands; it is hundreds of thousands or millions of network event logs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You use algorithms, smart software, to try to remove the bulk of them and identify suspected intrusions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But what you are worried about are not the ones that sort of deface your page and make you lose face but does not really affect you.

speaker: The Chairman
text: What you are worried about is cyber attack, things that can burrow into your systems, steal secrets or have a trigger at a particular time to render you defenceless.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There is structure, there is organisation, and much of it is what we call "security by design".

speaker: The Chairman
text: You design security into your networks even as you build them.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You can address these questions, as I have said, at the national level to CSA.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For the SAF, we expect to use more artificial intelligence and better data analytics to detect and respond to these cyber threats.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will build greater security into our software design, shore up the defences in our network architecture to make them more resistant and resilient to cyberattacks.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There will also be substantial investment into developing more and better-trained cyber defence personnel.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The SAF will work with the national CSA.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We spend a significant amount of our resources to maintain a strong defence but, even so, Singapore cannot face our security threats alone.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is foolhardy to try, and we will fail.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For example, to stop the spread of terrorism globally, we are stepping up our intelligence-sharing with our neighbours in Malaysia and Indonesia, and partners, such as the US and Australia, so that they can provide us with early warning and help us apprehend suspects that intend to do us harm.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is particularly important as militants have been using Southeast Asia as a transit point.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Beyond intelligence, we continue to build up enduring partnerships to strengthen regional security.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng and Mr Vikram Nair asked about our defence diplomacy efforts.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are friends with all and we cultivate relations with all, and we continue to build good ties with our closest neighbours, the Malaysian Armed Forces (MAF) and the TNI, the Indonesian National Defence Forces.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will also be celebrating the 40th anniversary of our defence relations with Brunei this year.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about China and the US.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is that close relationship with the US which has given us access to much-needed training space and high-end defence technology.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Whether it is our F-16, F-15, Chinook or Apache helicopters, our pilots train extensively in the US and they are given access to training areas many times the size of Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We agreed on a Four-Point Consensus for our military ties in 2014, to "promote confidence building… and strengthen practical cooperation".

speaker: The Chairman
text: With China, we introduced a new bilateral naval exercise series named Maritime Cooperation last year.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will build on these initiatives to encourage China to continue to play a peaceful and constructive role in the region.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng asked about Australia, on the CSP.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The defence relationship is a very important one.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Many SAF servicemen go to Exercise Wallaby, train in sizeable areas and we hope that this partnership will take us even further in personnel exchanges, counter-terrorism and R&D collaborations, through CSP that the two Prime Ministers endorsed last year.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Apart from our bilateral efforts, some Members have asked, as Mr Baey Yam Keng did, about the Shangri-La Dialogue and ADMM.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some Members have asked why we engage in these.

speaker: The Chairman
text: To paraphrase Churchill, "jaw-jaw is better than war-war".

speaker: The Chairman
text: Yes, this requires effort but, more importantly, coming together as a defence community promotes a rules-based security architecture, things that we can agree on, that are underpinned by international law and which create opportunities for dialogue and practical cooperation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Sometimes, it helps us, as some Members rightly pointed out, in responding to contingencies and crises like HADR.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It will take us a long time before we think of ourselves to be anything like NATO, and I am not even sure if the NATO structure is optimal for ASEAN.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We cooperate in partnerships with the understanding that it cannot mean that you subsume your sovereignty or your control of your military forces to other countries.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Where we can, we will cooperate and have dialogue.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Because just as damaging as physical harm, extremists can sow deep mistrust among Singaporeans and weaken our social cohesion.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The crucial question is this: after an extremist attack, will it splinter our society?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Will it paralyse Singaporeans and sow discord through fear?

speaker: The Chairman
text: We want to hear what Singaporeans hope to do to strengthen Total Defence and encourage more ground-up ideas.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Mohamad Maliki and Senior Minister of State Ong Ye Kung are leading these efforts and will share more about our SGFuture engagements later.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked if MINDEF or SAF should do more, whether it is a Defence White Paper or other aspects, to shore up support by Singaporeans and external countries in terms of our defence capabilities or defence intentions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: How we do it effectively, we can discuss.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But I would say that we conduct periodic polls – these are sometimes population surveys.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Thankfully, the support for defence has been very high.

speaker: The Chairman
text: At the core of Total Defence is societal trust – trust among one another as citizens, trust between commanders and soldiers, trust between the Government and people, trust between the SAF and those we promise to protect.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The SAF knows that it can only build this trust by living by its values.

speaker: The Chairman
text: One core value which all soldiers pledge is to defend Singapore with their lives.

speaker: The Chairman
text: SAF commanders and soldiers must put Singapore and Singaporeans first, above their own well-being, whether it is in training or operations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For MAJ Adrian Quek and MAJ Spencer Ler, let me just say, it would not be an exaggeration to say that probably their lives flashed before their eyes and their lives were at actual risk – it could have been their last flight.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In the meantime, while they were in free fall, they manoeuvred the helicopter down to an open field away from buildings.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The pilots survived and, more importantly, no civilians were injured.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We see this duty to put others before self, exemplified by our own NSFs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The recruit had accidentally released the hand grenade lever.

speaker: The Chairman
text: As many Members here who have done National Service know, when you release the lever, you throw the grenade, because that is when the grenade is activated.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This officer did not panic, immediately instructed the recruit to throw the grenade, then shielded the recruit as he pulled both of them down behind the concrete walls.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I wish I could promise Singaporeans that risks do not exist for our SAF soldiers who are asked to protect Singaporeans, who are asked to train hard and conduct missions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But all of you know that risks exist for all militaries – whether it is helicopters, infantry or ships.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will do all that we can to carry out our training and missions safely, because each life in Singapore is precious.

speaker: The Chairman
text: He was an NSman; after the incident, he decided to sign on and be a regular.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am very happy he joined the SAF.

speaker: The Chairman
text: These two pilots and this officer exemplify the core value of selfless service in the SAF.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I again ask and thank Members of this House and Singaporeans for their unstinting support and commitment to maintain our strong defence.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With Singaporeans strongly behind and with us, the SAF will respond decisively to all those who seek to do us harm and protect this precious island we call home.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In addition to having cutting-edge capabilities, a key element in maintaining a strong and professional armed forces is effective training.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: At MINDEF's COS debate in 2015, Minister Ng Eng Hen also said that the SAF had consistently benchmarked with militaries from other advanced countries and tested its systems through realistic training and real operations.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: He also discussed ways in which MINDEF and SAF had been prudent in their land use for training space.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Given Singapore's land constraints and the increasing complexity in the battlefield, in what new ways is SAF improving its training and learning systems in a way that overcomes resource constraints?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How is SAF ensuring that our servicemen maintain a high-level of operational readiness?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It bears repeating that NSmen are frontline soldiers and training must be taken seriously.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: However, for some soldiers, there are some areas of the NS training cycle that can be improved, subject to operational and budgetary exigencies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This would have the advantage of ensuring that the fitness levels of NSmen remain relatively high with a less steep physical training curve when preparing for the Individual Physical Proficiency Tests (IPPTs) or in-camp trainings (ICTs).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Some clock many low-key ICTs and fewer high-key ones, leading to a long wait before they are emplaced on MINDEF's reserve list.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is not surprising as a lot of our training is done overseas in view of the shortage of training grounds in Singapore, with the SAF going to places such as Germany, France, Australia, Thailand, India, Taiwan, Thailand, Brunei, New Zealand and the US, amongst others, in addition to ad hoc exercises with countries like China.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is inevitable that with such a high training tempo, accidents and mishaps can happen, in spite of the SAF's best efforts and the best efforts of the commanders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A section or a part of all open houses and public outreach campaigns can be dedicated to this purpose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While the information may not attract as many viewers as a Leopard tank on display, it would be an important reflection of MINDEF's commitment to safe and tough training in a realistic environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: For Singapore, our position at the crossroads of global trade and travel makes it a very strategic as well as a very vulnerable location.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Thus, in defending our nation, every effort, every individual counts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The SAF Volunteer Corps (VC) was introduced to enable persons who are not eligible for National Service to come forward to serve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: They are altruistic individuals and they act as our defence ambassadors, doing so voluntarily.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Can MINDEF update us on the initial batches of the Volunteer Corps?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Also, are there refinements needed to the scheme?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We also welcome the many advocates who support our National Service and defence movement in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: These persons and organisations are representatives from businesses, institutions, individuals and even small and medium enterprise (SME) employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How does MINDEF plan to continue to engage this important group of people and organisations and continue to strengthen our relationship with them into the future?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our NSmen form the backbone of our national defence system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a small country with an ageing population, we have to plan well to enable each serviceman to maximise his potential in protecting Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To fulfil their duties, our servicemen have to make a lot of sacrifices, take time from their studies, work and family life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, it is only appropriate that they be given due recognition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I was glad that CSNS was set up to examine how the NS system can be strengthened for the future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, MINDEF and MHA adjusted the pre-enlistment medical screening and administration schedule to enlist servicemen between four to six months.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on new initiatives by CSNS?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How has MINDEF continued its efforts to recognise the contributions of our NSmen?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They are all part of the Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Every Singaporean will know of someone serving or have served NS.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That someone may be a father, husband, brother, son or, for some, even grandson.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Occasionally, we are reminded of NS when we turn on our TV or radio.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We hear the broadcast about mobilisation, of in-camp training as well as mobilisation of resources with certain call signs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But beneath this calm and peaceful environment, thousands of men are donned in their green fatigues or pixelated uniforms on land, air and sea.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: A small part of them are professional soldiers but the bulk are our operationally-ready NSmen.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They have trained hard in all aspects of warfare, sometimes in the day and other times at night.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some would go overseas to train in various terrains, brave the thunderstorms during the monsoon season, or brave the gales and high seas, jumping off the plane with parachute and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Combat ration and cup noodles are luxuries during field training.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Sometimes, night becomes day and day becomes night.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: When in uniform, you do not worry about time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Your focus is achieving your mission, meeting your combat objectives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Well, I know all these because we have been there, done that with our fellow NSmen.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am still an active NS Navy medical officer.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Because we have a strong defence force as a foundation, this peace and security allows us to prosper and thrive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our NSmen answered to the call of the nation and serve in various vocations in the armed forces a few weeks annually.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During those few weeks, they will miss their families; their work will be shouldered by colleagues at their workplaces.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: NS has done a lot for our country.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Apart from putting up a strong defence force, NS also builds up a strong spirit of camaraderie – a Singapore identity among the men.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: NS is a platform that allows men to gel, eat, sleep and train together regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: NS is a passage, a bonding experience, for many Singaporeans across all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Intake after intake, our NSmen have answered to the call of duty.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Their competence and commitment are, indeed, qualities that would make every employer proud.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our men have undertaken so many missions, from humanitarian missions in the aftermath of natural disasters to participating in United Nations multinational military missions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since they have spent their youth defending our country, it is only right for the country to take care of them when they are old.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As NSmen form the majority of personnel in our defence force, they are assets to our defence.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is also important to provide training and develop our NSmen both professionally and personally.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What are the programmes available in this aspect and what can MINDEF do more in this area?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This condition can be debilitating over the long term and affect the ability to perform duties or work after leaving the service.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, Singapore spends large amounts on defence annually.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: How do we allocate funds to ensure that our NSFs and NSmen are adequately covered?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: How does MINDEF advise its members on SAF Group Insurance and ascertain that they are adequately insured?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: An injured or disabled person may need long-term care, equipment or facilities that go beyond medical services or prosthetics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This may drain the family financially and emotionally and may even require a family member to leave work to provide long-term care.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: How does MINDEF assess if the permanent loss of income and the cost of care for the lifetime of a disabled person are adequately covered?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, does the compensation framework take into consideration cases where injured service personnel are ineligible for insurance coverage after they leave the service or are forced to pay much higher premiums?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today, extremists are influenced by misinformation and wrong religious teachings to cause harm to innocent people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The change of tactics by these extremists to attack soft attacks, such as concert halls and cafes, has posed new challenges to the security forces of many countries and their people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides causing physical damage to property and killing innocent lives, these terrorist attacks have also affected the trust among different races and religions or between the government and its people.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thus, many countries are stepping up their anti-terrorism efforts to cope with these new threats.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Likewise, in Singapore, our Government has been strengthening our Total Defence capabilities to protect Singaporeans and prepare them for such attacks.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I understand that SG Secure will be conducting EP skills training in the community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that Singaporeans will adopt a more serious attitude to learn and practise these skills properly.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: EP skills will make a difference between life and death in times of emergencies.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: On Total Defence, we face a growing threat of extremist ideologies that threaten to undermine our multiracial and multi-religious harmony and divide us.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What role can Total Defence play in strengthening our resilience against such threats?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What are MINDEF's efforts in fostering Singaporeans' commitment to Total Defence?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Threats and challenges to our security continue to evolve.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
